Advanced: losses, two-candidate learning and paper settings

The input and coefficients are displayed in each exercise below.

The earlier coefficients were illustrative values. Learning requires scoring the prediction against a target and adjusting coefficients to reduce loss. Training from scratch typically starts with small random values and repeatedly compares predictions with targets in the data.

Align input and target by one position

Putting the answer into its own input position would let the model copy it. The input is context already available at that position; the target is the following token.

PositionDecoder inputTargetAvailable input
1startIstart
2Iwentstart, I
3wentto schoolstart, I, went
4to schoolendstart, I, went, to school

Training knows the targets and can compute all four positions together. But if input position 1 reads “I” at position 2, it sees its own answer. The causal mask blocks that route. Each position’s vocabulary distribution is scored against its target.

How wrong, as one number

Before anything can be corrected, how wrong it was has to be measured.

The last thing the model produces is a probability for each candidate next word. Take a small vocabulary with I / went / to school / end. After “I”, the target is the second candidate, went. These loss-training probabilities are a separate arithmetic example, not the connected block’s prediction.

Move the loss yourself

Computed example

See how loss −ln grows when less probability is assigned to the target. You directly edit an illustrative prediction; the other three probabilities keep their proportions and make the total 1.

Candidate order: 0 = I · 1 = went · 2 = to school · 3 = end. The target here is went.

probability on the right word: 0.60 → −ln(0.60) = 0.511

Optional: compare a softened target distribution

Compare a target with probability 1 only on the answer against one that shares some probability across all candidates. At ε = 0 the two losses coincide.

Try this Take the probability from 0.9 down to 0.1. The loss does not grow evenly; it gets steeper and steeper. That is the left end of the curve.

This is one position. A translated sentence has many, each giving a value like this; they are averaged into one loss per sentence, and the sentences processed together are combined into the single number that training pushes down.

First lower the probability of correct candidate went from 0.6 to 0.1. A worse prediction should receive a larger loss. Move it back towards 1 and the loss approaches 0.

Probability given to correct wentScored lossInterpretation
10All probability on the correct candidate
0.6About 0.511Some probability missing from the answer
0.1About 2.303Very low probability on the answer
Why does correct probability 0.6 receive loss 0.511?

Use the inverse of the exponential from softmax. Since e−0.511≈0.6e^{-0.511} \approx 0.6e−0.511≈0.6, the answer to “what power of e gives 0.6?” is about −0.511. That question is the natural logarithm ln. Reverse the sign to get score 0.511.

loss=−ln⁡(probability given to the answer)=−ln⁡(0.6)≈0.511\text{loss} = -\ln(\text{probability given to the answer}) = -\ln(0.6) \approx 0.511loss=−ln(probability given to the answer)=−ln(0.6)≈0.511

ln names the inverse exponential calculation; the minus sign reverses its sign. This loss grows as the probability of the answer approaches 0. Confident wrong predictions receive a larger penalty; learning tries to reduce it.

What about the words that were not the answer?

Pair target shares (0, 1, 0, 0) with prediction (0.1, 0.6, 0.2, 0.1): 0×(−ln 0.1) + 1×(−ln 0.6) + 0×(−ln 0.2) + 0×(−ln 0.1). Only went’s term survives. The full expression abbreviates the sum of those four terms:

loss=−∑itiln⁡(pi)\text{loss} = -\sum_{i} t_i \ln(p_i)loss=−i∑​ti​ln(pi​)

tit_iti​ is how much of the answer sits on word iii and pip_ipi​ is what the model gave it. Writing the answer as “1 on went, 0 elsewhere” makes every term with ti=0t_i = 0ti​=0 vanish, leaving only the term for the right word — hence −ln⁡(pright)-\ln(p_{\text{right}})−ln(pright​).

And the probabilities sum to 1, so they are tied together. Raising the right one forces the others down. Watching the right word handles the rest.

Which way to nudge

With the loss in hand, the next question is which direction reduces it.

If nudging one entry of WQW_QWQ​ upwards makes the loss larger, that entry should come down; if the loss falls, it should go up. Working out, for every entry, which way the loss moves when it changes slightly, gives the gradient.

Not just WQW_QWQ​. Every head’s WQW_QWQ​, WKW_KWK​, WVW_VWV​, the WOW_OWO​ that joins them, the two feed-forward matrices, the γ\gammaγ and β\betaβ of every normalization, all six layers’ worth, and the embedding table too: learned parameters are adjusted together. Scores S and shares A are computed results, not independently learned weight tables. The base model has about 65 million of them.

Every entry is then moved a little in the opposite direction. How much “a little” is comes from the learning rate.

This example and full backpropagation

Below, we calculate a derivative and update one weight. Backpropagation through all of attention, FFN and normalization is outside this example.

From a gradient to one actual update

Start with just one weight w. Multiply input 1 by w to make two logits (w, 0), with “went” first as the target and “to school” second as the alternative. This is a separate two-candidate, one-weight practice. At w = 0, softmax(0, 0) = (0.5, 0.5), and loss is −ln 0.5 ≈ 0.693.

Start with input 1, then change only the input to 0 or −1. The same coefficient’s output and update direction depend on what it multiplies.

Actually update one weight

Two candidates · one coefficient · computed loss and update

This separate exercise reduces the candidates after I to went and to school. Multiply x by w to score the correct candidate went; the other score is 0. Compute probabilities and loss from those two scores. It does not update the earlier full block.

Input × coefficient: 1 × (0.000) = 0.000 → two scores (0.000, 0) → P(went) = 0.500 → loss = 0.693147

Compare the loss with the coefficient 0.001 lower or higher.

wLoss L
−0.0010000.693647
0.0000000.693147
0.0010000.692647

Loss difference ÷ coefficient difference = (0.692647 − 0.693647) ÷ 0.002 = −0.500000

Analytic gradient g: −0.500000

Proposed update: w − ηg = 0.000 − 0.20 × (−0.500) = 0.100

P(went): 0.500 → 0.525 · L: 0.693147 → 0.644397

Updates applied: 0

Input 1 moves the coefficient up; input −1 moves it down. With input 0 the score cannot change with w, so the gradient is 0. Predict the direction before applying. This updates one weight; it is not backpropagation through an entire LLM.

With initial input 1, applying the update gives coefficient 0 → 0.1, correct probability 0.5 → about 0.525, and loss 0.693 → about 0.644. Expand the direction and step-size calculation below.

Which way should a loss change of −0.001 move the coefficient?
Small change to wLoss against the correct answer
−0.001About 0.693647
0About 0.693147
+0.001About 0.692647

Increasing w lowers the loss. Divide the loss change, about −0.001, by the weight change 0.002 to obtain a slope of about −0.5. In the lab, keep input 1 first and change w to inspect probability and loss. Then set the input to 0: any w still gives logits (0, 0). Set input to −1 and increasing w lowers the correct logit, so the update direction reverses.

Now abbreviate the calculation. L names the measured loss; w is the coefficient multiplying the input. Dividing the small loss change by the weight change gave −0.5. The rate as this interval shrinks is a derivative. Holding other values fixed and measuring it for w alone is written ∂L/∂w. It names the direction and rate you just observed when changing w.

  1. Direction as a number. Gradient g = −0.5. With input 1, this two-candidate example gives P(went) − 1 = 0.5 − 1.
  2. Step size. Choose learning rate 0.2. Its formula name is η.
  3. Take the opposite step. New w = 0 − 0.2 × (−0.5) = 0.1. Abbreviate as w ← w − ηg; the arrow assigns the new value.
  4. Compute again. Input×new w → logits → softmax → P(went)≈0.525 → loss≈0.644. The multiplication coefficient changed; probability was not edited directly.
const probabilities = softmaxRow([w, 0]).probabilities;
const gradient = probabilities[0] - 1; // derivative for this example with input 1
const nextWeight = w - learningRate * gradient;

Unlike moving a probability slider in the loss experiment, this updates a weight and computes new probabilities. The analytic derivative can be compared with the finite-difference slope. Actual backpropagation propagates derivatives along the computation graph rather than perturbing every weight separately. This experiment does not execute all the weights, data or backpropagation of a real LLM.

Optional: soften the target distribution with label smoothing

Teaching it not to be too sure

The paper adds one thing here. Rather than “1 on went and 0 elsewhere”, it takes a little of that certainty away.

the answer=(0.025,  0.925,  0.025,  0.025)\text{the answer} = (0.025,\; 0.925,\; 0.025,\; 0.025)the answer=(0.025,0.925,0.025,0.025)

εls=0.1\varepsilon_{ls} = 0.1εls​=0.1 has been removed and shared evenly across all four words, 0.025 each. The right word is one of the four, so it gets 0.025 back: 0.9+0.025=0.9250.9 + 0.025 = 0.9250.9+0.025=0.925. This is label smoothing.

Scoring the default prediction against the two target distributions gives 0.511 and 0.628. This compares different scoring targets; other predictions can have a lower smoothed loss. The paper’s report of worse perplexity and better BLEU after training is a separate experimental observation, not a proof from this one prediction.

The paper reports improved BLEU under its experimental conditions. This small probability example alone does not establish an improvement in translation quality for every model.

What the paper measured

Turning label smoothing off (εls=0\varepsilon_{ls} = 0εls​=0) drops BLEU from 25.8 to 25.3. Turning it up to 0.2 gives 25.7, also slightly down. 0.1 sits between them.

The learning rate does not stay put

At the start the weights are meaningless random numbers, and a large step from there lands somewhere arbitrary and far away. So training starts slowly, moves boldly once things have settled, and shortens the stride again towards the end so it does not overshoot a good spot. That is why the paper’s learning rate is not a fixed number but changes as training goes on.

One training step computes the loss for one batch of sentences and updates the weights once.

How does the learning rate rise to step 4000 and then fall?

At the base settings, step 1000 gives about 0.000175, step 4000 about 0.000699, and step 16000 about 0.000349. First compare these points on the curve. The formula chooses the smaller of an increasing and a decreasing rule.

lrate=dmodel−0.5⋅min⁡(step−0.5,  step⋅warmup−1.5)lrate = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min\left(step^{-0.5},\; step \cdot warmup^{-1.5}\right)lrate=dmodel−0.5​⋅min(step−0.5,step⋅warmup−1.5)

Whichever of the two terms inside the min⁡\minmin is smaller wins.

  • Early on the right-hand one, step⋅warmup−1.5step \cdot warmup^{-1.5}step⋅warmup−1.5, is smaller, so the rate climbs in proportion to the step.
  • Past 4000 steps the left-hand one, step−0.5step^{-0.5}step−0.5, takes over and the rate falls as one over the square root of the step.

The highest point is at exactly 4000 steps, about 7.0×10−47.0 \times 10^{-4}7.0×10−4.

Optional: the paper’s data, hardware and training conditions

How it was actually trained

The conditions the paper records. When the last section compares this model as “better and cheaper”, the cost figures come from the hardware and hours listed here.

Two words in the table first. The model does not correct itself after every sentence; many sentences are bundled, their loss measured together, and WWW corrected once. The bundle is a batch, and processing one batch and correcting WWW once is one step, the stepstepstep in the learning-rate formula. The sentence pairs are not the model’s own: they are text people had already translated (parliamentary proceedings, news), paired sentence by sentence, in the standard sets released each year by the WMT translation competition, which is what lets papers compare on equal terms. The newstest sets later are that competition’s test sets.

Data (En→De)4.5M sentence pairs, vocabulary 37 000
Data (En→Fr)36M sentences, vocabulary 32 000
One batchabout 25 000 source and target tokens each
Hardware8 P100 GPUs
Base model0.4 s per step × 100K steps ≈ 12 hours
Big model1.0 s per step × 300K steps ≈ 3.5 days
Adam (the update rule; it sets a separate step size per weight from its recent gradients; not covered here)β1=0.9\beta_1 = 0.9β1​=0.9, β2=0.98\beta_2 = 0.98β2​=0.98, ε=10−9\varepsilon = 10^{-9}ε=10−9
Warm-up4000 steps
Dropout0.1 (10% of the values zeroed at random)

Training loss can fluctuate between batches. Stopping can depend on validation trends and a chosen budget; the paper reports 100K base-model steps and 300K big-model steps. Once trained, weights are frozen and dropout is switched off. Deterministic decoding repeats its choice under the same conditions; sampling can differ with unchanged weights.

Dropout is not covered here

A model that starts leaning on a few routes through itself memorises the training data and weakens on new sentences. To prevent that, dropout randomly sets some values to zero during training, so no route can be relied on.

The paper measured it: turning dropout off drops BLEU from 25.8 to 24.6. That is a large difference for something this article only names in passing.

Check your understanding

Check Should the target to school be appended before computing its prediction probability?

Answer and reasoning

No. The input is I / went and the target is a separate label. Use its current probability, about 71.8%, to compute loss, then update a readout coefficient opposite to its gradient.

Interpret results: evaluation conditions, cost and limits

Comparison values, reference shares, content, final representations and vocabulary probabilities formed one computation. Each appended chunk led to a new prediction. These probabilities select a next chunk; they do not give the probability that generated content is factual.

Evaluate models using prediction loss, accuracy and compute cost on the same data under the same conditions. The optional material below examines translation evaluation and the paper’s experiments.

Advanced: the paper’s translation evaluation, experiments and cost

The input and coefficients are displayed in each exercise below.

That is the architecture. Now for what it actually achieved.

What BLEU is

Nobody can read and grade thousands of translated sentences by hand, and papers need one number they can compare. BLEU is that number. It compares the machine’s sentence with a human one and counts how much of it overlaps, on a scale from 0 to 100 where higher is better.

It is not a perfect measure. A correct translation using different words scores low, and an awkward one reusing the right words can score high. But for comparing models under the same conditions it is serviceable, which is why it is used. So 100 is not the target to read it against: a human translation also loses points wherever its word choice differs from the reference. It can receive a lower score despite being a good translation. What matters is the gap between models scored on the same data. The significance of a gap depends on the dataset, evaluation procedure and repeated-run variation.

Score and cost together

Table 2 of the paper does not report scores alone. It puts the training cost alongside them, because that is the argument being made.

Switch the language pair

Table 2 of the paper

language pair

The paper's claim is "better and cheaper", so score and cost sit on one chart. The points are Table 2 of the paper and the horizontal axis is the authors' estimate of training cost. These are transcribed, not computed on this page.

English → German highest: Transformer (big) at 28.4

Try this Switch to French. The base model scores below the earlier models there; only the big model is ahead. For German both are ahead. The same architecture, and a different picture per language pair.

On English to German, Transformer (big) leads at 28.4. The previous best was 26.36, from an ensemble of several models, so this is more than 2 ahead. An ensemble runs several separately trained models at once and averages their next-word probabilities; it gains a little and costs that many times more to train and to run. The point is that one Transformer beat it.

The base model is the more striking row. At 27.3 it passes every previously published single model and ensemble, with an estimated training cost of 3.3×10183.3 \times 10^{18}3.3×1018. Compared with the two ensembles with reported costs in Table 2, this is about 23–55 times lower: divide 7.7×10197.7 \times 10^{19}7.7×1019 and 1.8×10201.8 \times 10^{20}1.8×1020 by the base-model cost.

The horizontal axis is an estimate, not a measurement

A FLOP is one addition or multiplication; 3.3×10183.3 \times 10^{18}3.3×1018 means about that many arithmetic operations over the whole of training. The authors did not measure FLOPs. A footnote says they computed training time × number of GPUs × an assumed sustained rate per GPU, listing those assumed rates as 2.8, 3.7, 6.0 and 9.5 TFLOPS for the K80, K40, M40 and P100. TFLOPS is not a total but a speed, how many trillion operations one GPU does per second, so the total is speed × time × GPUs.

Good enough to compare orders of magnitude between models; not a precise figure.

Where the paper disagrees with itself

The English-to-French score appears twice, differently.

The abstract and Table 2 give Transformer (big) as 41.8. The body of §6.1 describes the same model as achieving “a BLEU score of 41.0”.

It was never corrected, not even in the v7 revision posted in 2023. This article quotes the 41.8 from Table 2 and records the discrepancy here.

Which parts actually mattered

With this many parts, the results alone cannot say which part earned the score. Change one thing and hold the rest fixed, and the difference in BLEU can be credited to that one thing. So the paper retrained the base model changing one thing at a time. That is Table 3.

What changedBLEUvs base
(the base setting)25.8—
one head24.9−0.9
32 heads25.4−0.4
dkd_kdk​ of 1625.1−0.7
2 layers23.7−2.1
8 layers25.5−0.3
dffd_{ff}dff​ of 409626.2+0.4
dropout off24.6−1.2
label smoothing off25.3−0.5
learned positions25.7−0.1

Some things fall out of that.

  • Depth matters most. Going from six layers to two costs 2.1.
  • Head count affects this experiment. One head and 32 heads scored below the eight-head base model. At a fixed total width, more heads reduce the coordinates per head, but this table does not establish that as the sole cause or that eight is always best.
  • Dropout matters more than you might expect. Turning it off costs 1.2.
  • Sinusoids or learned positions make almost no difference. 0.1 apart.

These numbers are not comparable with Table 2

Table 3 reports BLEU on the development set (newstest2013); Table 2 reports it on the test set (newstest2014).

The checkpoint conditions also differ. Table 2 averages the last five checkpoints for the base model and 20 for the big model. Table 3 uses no checkpoint averaging (sections 6.1 and 6.2). The 25.8 and 27.3 scores therefore cannot be explained by the dataset alone or treated as an improvement between these tables.

And on something other than translation

To show this was not a translation-only architecture, the paper tried one more task: working out the grammatical structure of English sentences: the tree that groups a sentence into phrases (“this chunk is a noun phrase, that one a verb phrase”). Written with brackets, that tree is a single line like (S (NP the cat) (VP sat)), which makes “English sentence → bracketed line” the same kind of job as translation.

A small four-layer model, trained on about 40 000 sentences — not much data. It scored an F1 of 91.3 (F1 combines precision and recall into one score, 100 being perfect), in line with models built specifically for that task over many years. Given more data it reached 92.7.

The point is that an architecture designed for translation was carried over almost unchanged and did this well.

The limits the paper names itself

The closing section lists what the authors wanted to do next, which read backwards is what they had not done.

  • Long inputs. As the end of the attention section noted, the score matrix is n×nn \times nn×n, so cost climbs quickly as sentences grow. The paper names restricted attention as a direction.
  • Things other than text. Images, audio and video are listed as plans.
  • Generation being sequential. Making it less so is set out as a goal.

These are research directions proposed in the paper at the time, rather than a complete list of improvements in current models.

That is the paper

The starting question was how context produces a next-token prediction.

From there we went through vectors and matrix products, the dot product and softmax, computed attention, combined heads and positions into one block, updated one coefficient, and chose chunks to extend a sentence.

What remains beyond this guide: full Transformer backpropagation, detailed dropout arithmetic, the full BLEU definition, and every change in modern models. One-weight updates and the basic GPT connection were worked through here.

Interpret the table yourself

Set the experiment to English→German. The base model’s 27.3 exceeds the earlier results and its estimated training cost is lower. Then switch to English→French. The base model’s 38.1 does not exceed every earlier score. Read data and conditions before reducing a model name to a single conclusion.

ItemQuestion to ask
Dataset and language pairIs this the same task and evaluation data?
Measured quantityTraining cost or the cost of generating a token?
MetricDoes BLEU measure translation overlap or factual accuracy?
Changed settingsDid coupled values such as head count and head width change together?
Scope of conclusionAn experimental observation or a guaranteed property of a calculation?
Why separate development and test data?

Data used to select settings or stopping points has already influenced model selection. Separate test data checks results after that selection. The difference between 25.8 and 27.3 on different datasets is therefore not an improvement attributable to the model. Repeated-run variation matters too.

Length costs and limits of the worked example

Dense attention’s score table has n × n cells for n tokens. Predict the cell count before doubling 3 tokens to 6.

Tokens nScore cells n²Relative to 3 tokens
391×
6364×
1214416×
Why does doubling tokens quadruple the score cells?

Three query rows paired with three key rows make 3×3=9 cells. Six of each make 6×6=36 cells. 6 is twice 3, but 36÷9=4. Both rows and columns doubled: 2×2=4. n names the token count; n² abbreviates n×n.

This computes score-table size. Total model cost also includes projections, FFN, block count and implementation choices. Small hand arithmetic does not verify a trained model’s language understanding or hardware speed.

Connect back to the first question

Context pieces become IDs and vectors; attention mixes information from other positions. FFN, residual and normalization transform that representation. A final readout and softmax produce vocabulary probabilities. Generation chooses and appends a token; training changes weights using target loss. Choose a connection you still cannot explain and revisit its experiment. Confirm arithmetic and conceptual understanding separately.

Check your understanding

Check Do BLEU 25.8 on development data and 27.3 on test data show that a model improved?

Answer and reasoning

No: the datasets differ. Compare under the same evaluation conditions. Head-count results are observations from this paper’s setup, not guarantees for every model.
